title: Drop Everything And Read - Or Teach?
author: Jen O'Sullivan
summary: Jen O'Sullivan asks whether the beloved Irish practice of Drop Everything and Read (DEAR) time earns its place in a crowded literacy curriculum, since fifteen minutes a day adds up to roughly forty-five hours a year. She organises the question into opportunity, experience and outcome. As opportunity, DEAR protects reading time at a moment of declining voluntary reading and may be the only reading time some children get. As experience, it differs sharply between proficient readers and struggling readers who pretend-read or keep switching books. As outcome, the research is underwhelming: a review of 14 studies found no meaningful benefit and a 2024 meta-analysis found a very small effect with effectively zero impact on comprehension. Drawing on Tim Shanahan, she notes the correlation between reading volume and skill runs both ways. Rather than abolishing DEAR, she suggests reshaping it, with independent reading built into explicit lessons, teacher check-ins and a set of reflective questions about what each child actually gets.
points: Distinguishing the opportunity DEAR provides, the experience each child has and the outcomes teachers want clarifies what the practice can and cannot deliver.
Struggling readers may spend DEAR time pretend reading or swapping books, so for them independent reading can become struggling alone.
Meta-analytic evidence shows little to no benefit of silent reading time for comprehension, though motivation and access to books remain legitimate aims.
De-implementation means weighing DEAR against the explicit fluency, spelling, vocabulary and writing instruction it displaces, not simply adding more practices.
Reshaping DEAR through guided independent reading within lessons, pre-reading support for some children and brief teacher check-ins can keep its benefits while reducing its risks.
quotes: DEAR time provides the opportunity for children to read but it doesn’t tell us what a child experiences during those fifteen minutes or what they gain from them.
For others, access to books and time to read should not be taken for granted. For these children, school might be the one place where both are consistently available.
From the teacher’s perspective, both children appear occupied but while one is absorbed in a story, the other is possibly counting down the minutes to when reading time is over.

This leaves us in an uncomfortable position: DEAR time might provide additional reading practice for children who can already read independently, while leaving struggling readers with the very task they find the most difficult.

A review carried out by Erbeli and Rice (2021) examined 14 experimental and quasi-experimental studies involving more than 10,000 students and found no meaningful beneficial effects of independent silent reading on reading outcomes.

Reading more may help children become stronger readers, but being a stronger reader may also lead children to read more! We cannot therefore assume that simply giving every child more time to read independently will produce the same benefits.
We cannot continue to add evidence-informed practices to literacy instruction without considering what they will replace.
De-implementation does not always mean eliminating a practice entirely. It can mean reducing it, reshaping it or replacing aspects that offer less value.
